Clinical Importance
The purpose of this case report is to highlight potential complications associated with intrathecal baclofen (ITB) 
administration in a patient with Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS)
Patient Case
HPI : A 54-year old female presented with high fevers and mental status changes attributed to urosepsis.
PMH :  SPS (anti-GAD 65 Ab+) diagnosed 2004, ITB pump placed 2004, rhabdomyolysis and baclofen pump failure 
(kinked tubing) 7/2009
SH : Resides in SNF , full assist with all ADLs, power wheelchair , Hoyer lift for transfers
Home medications : clonazepam 1mg po q8hr alternated with diazepam 1mg po q8hr , ITB 899mcg/day
Hospital Day 2
• Despite appropriate antibiotics, patient remained febrile (105-107°F) and developed tachycardia, autonomic instability, 
increasing episodes of severe spasticity and rigidity, and an elevated CPK
• Symptoms now recognized as acute baclofen withdrawal
• High-dose oral baclofen and IV diazepam started
Hospital Day 3
• Intubation and mechanical ventilation now necessary to maintain patent airway and allow for high-dose sedation 
needed to control rigidity and severe spastic episodes
• High-dose midazolam and propofol infusions, in addition to oral baclofen and IV diazepam, now required
Hospital Day 5-10
• Imaging, interrogation, and open surgery of the pump system revealed system failure due to catheter-pump 
disconnection 
• Catheter and implanted pump replaced and ITB therapy restarted
Hospital Day 11-79
•  ITB titrated in increasing, step-wise fashion to achieve symptom control
• She required high-dose infusions of midazolam, fentanyl, and propofol as well as high-dose oral baclofen, tizanidine, 
dantrolene, and cyproheptadine for symptom control and to allow for adequate ventilation while ITB dose titrated
• Weaning of intravenous and oral agents complicated by frequent episodes of acute stiffening, spasms, and autonomic 
instability, requiring additional sedative rescue doses
• Autonomic instability required intermittent use of pressors and transcutaneous pacing
• Recovery complicated by episodes of urosepsis, bacteremia, and pneumonia
Hospital Day 80
• Discharged to L T AC with antispasmodic regimen consisting of ITB 1200mcg/day, baclofen 30mg po q4hr , diazepam 
5mg po q6hr , tizanidine 4mg po q6hr , and cyproheptadine 4mg po q6hr
Severe, Prolonged Baclofen Withdrawal Following a Second  
Catheter Failure in a Patient with Stiff Person Syndrome 
Cara McDaniel, PharmD, BCPS  •  Thomas Jefferson University Hospital, Philadelphia, PA
JG 11-1300
MC 10-03011
Discussion
• Chronic baclofen exposure causes GABA B  receptor down-regulation. Sudden withdrawal can lead to an 
exaggerated CNS excitatory state and cause excess serotonin release.
• Autonomic dysfunction, common in SPS patients, paired with acute baclofen withdrawal may further induce 
autonomic failure, adding to the severity of withdrawal symptoms.
• Infection may exacerbate underlying CNS excitation and autonomic instability.
• Multimodal therapy may be necessary to manage severe withdrawal syndromes.
• GABA B  down-regulation from chronic baclofen use paired with autonomic dysfunction and decreased GABA 
receptor expression and function in SPS may explain why this patient experienced prolonged recovery and required 
multiple high dose agents to achieve symptom control.
Final Comments 
• Baclofen withdrawal syndrome can be a life-threatening complication of ITB therapy. Quick recognition and 
aggressive management are essential.

• Intrathecal drug delivery systems represent a significant challenge to the medical community. Knowledge and 
management of these systems is often limited to specialists who deal directly with their placement, function,  
and maintenance.
• Pharmacists can play a large role in the care of patients who are receiving drugs via intrathecal drug delivery 
systems. Pharmacists can offer alternative drug dosing and therapies if pump failure occurs.
References
1.  Bardutzky J, Tronnier V, Schwab S. et al. Intrathecal baclofen for stiff-person syndrome: life-threatening intermittent catheter leakage. Neurology 2003;60:1976-78.
2.  Coffey RJ, Edgar TS, Francisco GE, et al. Abrupt withdrawal from intrathecal baclofen: recognition and management of a potentially life-threatening syndrome. Arch Phys Med 
Rehabil 2002;83:735-41.
3.  Dalakas MC. Advances in the pathogenesis and treatment of patients with stiff person syndrome. Curr Neurol Neurosci Rep 2008;8(1):48-55.
4.  Douglas AF , Weiner HL, Schwartz DR. Prolonged intrathecal baclofen withdrawal syndrome. J Neurosurg 2005;102:1133-36.
5.  Hansen CR, Gooch JL, Such-Neibar T. Prolonged, severe intrathecal baclofen withdrawal syndrome: a case report. Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2007;88:1468-71.
6.  Meinck HM, Tronnier V, Rieke K, et al. Intrathecal baclofen treatment for stiff-man syndrome: pump failure may be fatal. Neurology 1994;44:2209-2210.
7.  Mitsumoto H, Schwartzman MJ, Estes ML, et al. Sudden death and paroxysmal autonomic dysfunction in stiff-man syndrome. J Neurol 1991;238:91-6.
8.  Mohammed I, Hussain A. Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal syndrome - a life-threatening complication of baclofen pump: a case report. BMC Clin Pharmacol 2004;4:6.
9.  Ross JC, Cook AM, Stewart GL, et al. Acute intrathecal baclofen withdrawal: a brief review of treatment options. Neurocrit Care 2010 Aug 18 [Epub ahead of print]
Disclosure
Cara McDaniel has nothing to disclose concerning possible financial or personal relationships with commercial entities that may have a direct or 
indirect interest in the subject matter of this presentation.
Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS)
• Rare, progressive disorder characterized by severe rigidity, painful spasms, and continuous motor unit activity
• Patients often have spontaneous disturbances in the autonomic nervous system
• Patients often possess antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), a rate-limiting enzyme needed in 
gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) production, as well as antibodies that lead to decreased expression and function 
of GABA receptors
Intrathecal Baclofen (ITB) Administration
• Employs an implantable drug delivery system 
– Intrathecal catheter , implanted pump, external computer program
• Advantage: 
– T argeted drug delivery to the site of action
– Continuous therapy
– Minimization of systemic adverse effects 
• Disadvantage: 
– Risk of catheter or pump failure 
– Requires expertise in system management, equipment, troubleshooting,  
and surgical intervention techniques
Complications Associated with Intrathecal Drug Administration
• Device Complications
– Battery malfunction, pump malfunction, programming error
• Catheter Complications
– Obstruction, dislocation, kinking, fracture
• Surgical Complications
– Bruising, bleeding, swelling, infection, CSF leak, headaches, paralysis
• Drug Overdose
• Drug Withdrawal
